text.en: The mela has finally come to town and Nita and Radha are getting ready to go. There is a lot of excitement. Dadiji, whose legs hurt, is persuaded to come too. Join the two families on their bus ride, their day at the mela and the safe way back home.

Nita and Radha are getting ready to go to the mela, and the whole house is excited. The mela is a little far from home, so they will go by bus. Dadiji has a bad leg, so at first she says she cannot come. Nita's father promises that the family will take care of her, and Dadiji agrees to go. Dadiji reminds the children to fill up their water bottles. A water bottle is something we should carry when we go out for a long day. Their neighbours Sneha and Rohit are joining them, and Mohan Chacha, Nita's father's brother, and his family are arriving by train. A mela is a gathering of many people.
The families go to the bus stop and Nita's father helps Dadiji walk slowly, holding her hand, to the stop. We should always help elders who find it hard to walk. In the bus the children are asked to sit on their seats and not to jump around. They are also told not to put their hands or heads out of the window, for safety. The bus goes through the city and reaches the big parade ground where the mela is held. We travel in many ways: on foot, by bus, train, autorickshaw, car, bicycle or boat. Mohan Chacha's family came by train and then by an autorickshaw.
At the entrance of the mela there is a map of the ground showing the stalls and where they are. A map helps us find our way. Near the map an ambulance, a police jeep and a fire engine are parked, so help is ready for an accident, an illness or a fire. There is also a 'Lost and Found' booth with volunteers. If someone gets lost, or loses something, they can go there. Mohan Chacha and Rohit hurry to get a wheelchair for Dadiji, so that she can enjoy the mela without getting tired.
Inside, the children see stalls with games, toys, sweets and many interesting things. They go to the toy stall and buy spinning tops, puppets, phirkis and dolls. They ride on the merry-go-round and the giant wheel. Sneha and Radha buy bangles and other trinkets. Then they go to see a magic show and enjoy it very much. A mela has many workers, such as the toy seller, bangle seller, puppeteer, halwai who makes sweets, mehendi artist, police officer, firefighter, medical attendant and volunteer, and each one does a useful job.
Mohan Chacha says they have had a lot of fun and now they should eat. But before eating the children must wash their hands properly, and they go to the water point. The children enjoy gol gappas, chaat, chhole kulche, hot jalebis with rabri, kulfi and many other tasty things. After eating they make sure they put all the waste in the dustbin. We must keep a place clean wherever we go. Washing hands before eating and using dustbins keeps us healthy and keeps the mela clean.
As they leave, Dadiji points out someone accompanying a police officer. The children answer that it is a police dog. Police dogs help the police to find lost things and people. They are trained and obey their handlers. Kumbh Mela is the world's biggest festival. It is the largest gathering of people and is held on the banks of the rivers Ganga, Yamuna, Godavari and Shipra, once in 12 years, in Haridwar, Prayagraj, Nashik and Ujjain. Melas bring people together to enjoy games, food, music and shopping, and to meet friends and relatives.
A sketch or map shows where places are. We can find a house, a police station or the parade ground on it, and trace the route from one place to another. We can draw our own sketch of the route from home to school and mark the places on the way. To stay safe while travelling we sit properly in a vehicle, never put our hands or heads out of the window, and hold an elder's hand in a crowd. We can look after our elders by helping them walk, offering them a seat, carrying their bag and talking politely to them.
How do you prepare yourself for a trip? Nita packs a special bag and Sneha checks that she has everything she needs before leaving. Bus number 401 stopped for them, and there was a seat reserved for older people, where Dadiji sat comfortably. Rohit's father asked for five full and four half tickets, because younger children pay a half ticket.
Have you ever been to a mela? Tell the class what you liked most there. Imagine you are Nita, Radha, Sneha or Rohit, and share the interesting things you would do in the mela. Ask the elders in your family how melas were different when they were young. Why are fire engines and ambulances present in a mela? They are there to help quickly if there is a fire or somebody is hurt.
Study the sketch, circle the houses of Rohit and Sneha and of Nita and Radha, and tell whose house is closer to the parade ground. Match each helper with the work: firefighter, volunteer, halwai, toy seller, puppeteer, bangle seller, police officer, medical attendant and mehendi artist. Draw and label the different vehicles that you see around your school and home.
With your teacher, organise a mock mela in your classroom with stalls, games, buyers and sellers. Use toys, puppets, play money, miniatures and clay models to set up your stalls, and take turns as buyer and seller. A mock mela teaches us to plan together, to share work and to be polite to everyone.

problem.en: Find your way on a mela map: how do we reach the food stalls from the entrance?

text.en: Find the entrance on the map and put your finger on it.

why.en: We always begin from where we are.

text.en: Move along the paths to the food stalls, noting what lies on the way, like the toy stall or the water point.

why.en: Noting places on the way helps us remember the route.

text.en: Say the route aloud: 'From the entrance, go past the Lost and Found booth and the toy stall to the food stalls'.

why.en: Saying the route aloud makes it easier to follow and to tell somebody else.

problem.en: Lost in a crowd: what should a child do?

text.en: Stop and stay where you are. Do not run around.

why.en: If you stay, the family can find you more easily.

text.en: Look for a police officer, a volunteer or the Lost and Found booth and ask for help.

why.en: Helpers wear uniforms or badges and are trained to help.

text.en: Tell them your name and your parents' names and wait until your family comes.

why.en: This helps the helper to find your family.

prompt.en: Tell a friend about the mela and how to stay safe there.

requiredIdeas.en: Mela has stalls, rides, shows and food
Map, Lost and Found, ambulance, police and fire engine are there to help
Wash hands before eating and put waste in dustbins
Sit properly in the bus and help elders

commonMisconceptions.en: A mela has nobody to help us if we get lost
It is fine to put our head out of the bus window

points.en: A mela is a gathering of many people with stalls, rides, games and food.
A map and a Lost and Found booth help us find our way and lost things.
An ambulance, a police jeep and a fire engine are at the mela for safety.
Wash your hands before you eat and put waste in the dustbin.
In a vehicle, sit properly and keep hands and heads inside the window.
We should look after our elders and help them.
